abstract: |
  Low-poly papercraft masks are distributed by their designers, for sale or free for personal
  use, as printable PDF templates. They are designed for
  printing and cutting by hand, and they carry assumptions that become drawbacks once a builder
  uses a cutting machine: edge numbers in a font too small to read (and to OCR), many small
  pieces and short seams that are hard to glue and keep closed, narrow glue tabs, a fixed paper
  size, a fixed colour per page, and no three-dimensional reference for where a piece goes. We
  describe an open-source pipeline that recreates such a template digitally, from the PDF the
  builder obtained from the designer, and then rebuilds it for fabrication. Edge numbers are read by OCR and
  corrected using the mirror symmetry of the mask; the pieces are folded into a 3D mesh that an
  interactive viewer shows piece by piece; the mesh is re-segmented into fewer, larger pieces with
  darts; tabs are regenerated wider; pieces are renumbered in a build order that keeps tabs
  reachable; and an evolutionary search nests the pieces on the builder's own paper size, with
  the side that carries each tab as a free variable. On one designer mask, free for personal use (a 21-sheet US Letter
  template with 180 pieces) the recreation has 113 pieces and 16 instead of 41 seams shorter than
  15 mm, while needing one Letter sheet fewer despite wider tabs. We close with a model of total build
  time for cutting-machine builds, where sheets are ordered so that the previous sheet can be
  glued while the next one cuts.

# Introduction

Papercraft masks and helmets made of low-poly cardstock are a popular craft. Designers sell them,
or give them away for personal use, as PDF templates: a set of printable pages with the unfolded pieces, cut lines, fold lines, glue
tabs and small numbers that tell the builder which edge glues to which. The format is made for a
home printer, scissors and a scoring tool. Many builders now own a cutting machine (Cricut,
Silhouette, Brother ScanNCut) that can cut, score and draw on cardstock, but the template is
still a picture: the machine cannot use it until someone traces it, and the template's design
choices, made for hand cutting, stay in place.

This paper is a case study of that gap. One of us downloaded a designer's template for a low-poly
Bowser mask and built it with a Cricut. Doing so exposed a list of practical problems that have
little to do with the quality of the design and a lot to do with the template being a fixed,
printed artefact (@sec-problem). We then describe an open-source pipeline,
`lowpoly-pdf-to-svg`, that recreates the template digitally and uses the recreation to fix those
problems (@sec-method), and we look at a part of the build that templates ignore entirely: the
time it takes, and how the order of the sheets changes it (@sec-time).

Contributions:

1. A list of the drawbacks of ready-made papercraft templates when the build uses a cutting
   machine, drawn from a full build and from builder forums.
2. A pipeline that turns a ready-made template into an editable, fabrication-ready model: OCR of
   edge numbers corrected by mirror symmetry, a folded 3D mesh, an interactive viewer with an
   assembly player, re-segmentation with darts, generated wider tabs, build-order numbering and
   evolutionary nesting with tab placement as a variable.
3. A model of total build time for cutting-machine builds, and sheet ordering that lets gluing
   overlap with cutting.
4. A position on reuse: the software works on a template the builder obtained legitimately (bought, or free for
   personal use), for personal edits;
   it does not redistribute the designer's PDF or pages.

# The problem: what a ready-made template gets in the way of {#sec-problem}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## To do
One short paragraph per drawback, each with the Bowser number and, where we have it, a builder
forum quote (paraphrased, with source). Keep the tone fair to the designer: these are properties
of the format, not of this design.
:::

**Numbers that are hard to read.** Every glue edge carries a number, and the matching edge on
another piece carries the same number. In the Bowser template there are 1,569 such numbers
*(check)*, printed in a very small font along the edge, sometimes rotated and sometimes
touching the line. They are hard for a person to find on a cut piece and hard for OCR: 82 of
them (5 %) were not read with confidence, and 675 needed a correction of some kind before every
edge had a partner *(check)*. For the builder the number also says little: it tells which two
edges meet, not where the piece goes on the mask.

**Many small pieces and short seams.** The template has 180 pieces on 21 sheets. Low-poly
detail such as the nose, teeth, eyebrows and hair is split into small pieces with short edges:
41 seams are shorter than 15 mm *(check: seam count from segment.py)*. A short seam has little
glue area, is hard to press closed from inside, and breaks first; in our build the green nose
came apart at exactly these seams.

**Narrow tabs.** The printed tabs are narrow and are drawn on one side of each seam. The builder
used 15 mm double-sided tape cut into strips, which wants 7.5 mm tabs, and wider flaps where the
load is high.

**A fixed paper size.** The template is laid out on US Letter. European cardstock is A4, which is
narrower and longer; pieces near the edge of a Letter page do not fit, and the pages cannot
simply be scaled without changing the size of the mask.

**A fixed colour per page.** Each page is one colour. Changing the colour of a few parts (here:
gold horns, rust hair and eyebrows, a red mouth, brown horn rings) moves pieces between colours,
so the designed pages cannot be cut as they are and have to be rearranged by hand.

**No 3D reference.** The template shows a picture of the finished mask and the flat pieces, but
not where a given piece sits, which side faces out, or what to glue first. Builders work this
out from the numbers.

**A fixed order.** Page order is the designer's layout order, not an order that is easy to
build. The builder found it much easier to assemble the hair and eyebrows first and then fit them
into the larger head pieces, while the tabs could still be reached and pressed.

# Method: recreating the template digitally {#sec-method}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## To do
Condense from `report/method.qmd` (vectorization, review) and the issues named in each
subsection. One own-drawn figure for the pipeline, one for the notation, one for the viewer
(screenshot of our own generated model, not the template).
:::

A pipeline figure (to draw) will show the stages. The input is the PDF the builder obtained and a short
YAML file per model (paper size, fold styles, colours). Everything after vectorization works on
our own representation, so later stages never need the PDF again.

## Vectorization and reading the numbers

Pages are rendered with `pdftoppm`, cut and fold lines are found with OpenCV (solid strokes are
cuts, dashed and dash-dot strokes are valley and mountain folds), and every dashed segment is
replaced by one straight fold line. Cut outlines are kept as polygons, since the model is
low-poly. Edge numbers are read with Tesseract plus a digit matcher, never traced as paths. A
semi-supervised check page shows the uncertain reads for confirmation.

## Mirror symmetry as a correction signal

A mask is mirror-symmetric, so almost every piece has a twin. The twin is found by matching the
face (tabs may differ), and every numbered edge on a piece has a mirrored edge on the twin with
the same length. This turns symmetry into a check on the reading: a number that has no partner,
pairs with an edge of a different length, or pairs differently from its twin's number is
flagged, and the twin's pairing suggests the correct value. On Bowser all 74 twin pairs were
matched *(check)*, and the remaining mismatched faces were repaired by mirror-averaging body
corners. Symmetry also catches tracing faults: a missing fold on one twin is copied from the
other.

## A 3D mesh and an interactive viewer

With every edge paired, the pieces are folded into a 3D mesh (fold3d): each piece is a set of
planar faces joined at its fold lines, and glued edges are brought together. The mesh drives a
local Three.js viewer in which the builder can click a piece in 3D and see it on the flat sheet
and vice versa, filter by cardstock, search by number, and switch the labels between the PDF
numbers and the new short labels.

## Re-segmentation with darts

The mesh no longer has to be cut where the designer cut it. Starting from the welded,
symmetrized mesh, pieces are merged (both twins at once) as long as the merged piece still
unfolds flat without overlap and fits on the sheet with a margin. Candidate partitions are scored
by short seams first, then tiny pieces, number of pieces, number of seams, darts and seam length;
the choice is made by set partitioning (HiGHS, or Gurobi) or by a random-key genetic algorithm
[@bean1994] that also accounts for sheets (next subsection). Where a merge would almost close a
cone, a thin dart is left: one side is cut and the slit is kept as a glue flap. This follows
the topological-surgery view of unfolding [@takahashi2011] and strip-based unfolding for
papercraft [@mitani2004], but with fabrication terms (seam length, sheet fit) in the objective.

| Model part | Pieces (PDF) | Pieces (recut) | Seams < 15 mm (PDF) | Seams < 15 mm (recut) |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Green (nose, snout) | 26 | 16 | 11 | 2 |
| Whole mask | 180 | 113 | 41 | 16 |

: Re-segmentation of the Bowser mask *(check; regenerate from segment/evolve summaries)*. {#tbl-resegment}

The remaining short seams sit on colour boundaries (white teeth against yellow, rust eyebrows
against green), where a cut is needed anyway.

## Wider tabs and flaps

Tabs are regenerated rather than traced: 7.5 mm along the whole glue edge (half of a 15 mm
tape strip), and 15 mm wide tongues on seams that carry load or are short. A tab never crosses a
fold of the face it glues onto; it is clipped there. Twins carry mirrored tabs, except where a
piece glues to its own twin, where tabs alternate sides. Which side of a seam gets the tab is a
free choice, and the nesting uses it.

## Nesting on the builder's paper, with tab side as a variable

Pieces are nested per colour on the builder's sheet size, here A4 instead of the template's
Letter, by the C++ nester `papercraft-nester`. Because each seam's tab can sit on either piece,
the outline of a piece is not fixed until the tabs are assigned; the evolutionary search treats
the tab side of each seam as part of the genome, next to the partition, and scores the sheet
count with a fast shelf-packing proxy, confirming the best candidates with the real nester
[cf. @jakobs1996 for genetic nesting of polygons]. On Bowser, nested on Letter for a like-for-like comparison, the recreation needs 21 sheets where
the template's pieces, re-nested after recolouring, needed 22 *(check)*, although every tab is
wider. The A4 run is still to do.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## Recolouring

Colours are assigned per piece in the YAML file, so a recolour is an edit and a re-nest, not a
manual rearrangement of pages. A palette in the YAML and recolouring in the viewer are planned
(#88).

## Notation and build-order numbering

The new labels replace the template's three-digit edge numbers with short two-character labels
in a 5 mm font, and each piece gets a piece number up to 10 mm high in its middle. Twins share
the number; the frame tells them apart: a circle on the copy on the wearer's right, a square on
the wearer's left (looking into the mask, circles are on the right; from outside, on the left), and a triangle (with an A prefix) for a piece that crosses the middle and so
exists once.

All marks are on the inside of the mask. The builder lays the cardstock good side down on the
cutting mat, so the machine's pen draws labels and numbers on the back, which becomes the inside;
the visible surface stays clean, as it would with a hand-cut template whose printed lines are
folded inwards. The viewer draws the labels on both sides of each face, so the builder can read
them while turning the model, from outside as well as through the neck opening.

Pieces are numbered in build order. The order sweeps from the parts farthest from the neck
towards the neck, adds twins together, and prefers continuing from the last step; so hair and
eyebrows come first and are fitted into the larger head pieces afterwards, while their tabs are
still reachable from the open side. On Bowser this gives 89 steps from 6 starting
sub-assemblies, with the neck rim last *(check)*. The viewer's Assemble player steps through
the order and outlines the pieces of each step on the model.

## Reuse and the designer's rights

The software is open source; the templates are not ours. The pipeline runs on a PDF the builder
bought, keeps the outputs local, and is meant for personal adaptation (paper size, colour,
stronger tabs, fewer pieces). It does not redistribute the PDF, the page images or the traced
pieces, and the public project site shows only counts and a generic example model.

# Cutting-machine build time {#sec-time}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## To do
This section depends on #87 (time model) and #86 (sheet order). Draft the model now; fill the
numbers once a few sheets and glue steps have been timed.
:::

A cutting machine is slow compared with a printer. Each sheet goes through several passes: cut,
valley score, mountain score and pen drawing, each with its own tool change, and the sheet has
to be loaded, unloaded and weeded. For Bowser the passes add up to 57 m of cutting, 38 m of
valley and 15 m of mountain scoring and 12 m of drawing over 21 sheets, plus pen-up travel
*(check)*. While the machine works on one sheet the builder glues the pieces of the previous
one, so the build is a two-stage flow shop: the machine is the first stage, gluing the second
[@johnson1954].

**Machine time per sheet.** For sheet $s$ and pass $p$,
$$T_s = t_{load} + \sum_{p} \left( \frac{L_{s,p}}{v_p} + \frac{D_{s,p}}{v_{travel}} + n_{s,p}\, t_{lift} + t_{tool} \right),$$
with drawn length $L$, travel $D$ and pen or blade lifts $n$ taken from the cut plan, and speeds
and constants fitted to timed sheets.

**Glue time per step.** For build step $j$, $G_j = a + b\,\ell_j + c\,k_j + d\,m_j$, with glued
length $\ell_j$, number of tabs $k_j$ and number of seams shorter than 15 mm $m_j$.

**Total time.** Step $j$ can start once all its pieces are cut and step $j-1$ is done. The total
build time is the makespan of the two stages. With colour-grouped sheets, the first sheets often
hold pieces that cannot be joined to anything yet, and the builder waits. Ordering the sheets
(and, inside the nester, choosing which pieces share a sheet) so that each sheet unlocks build
steps reduces the idle time (#86).

| Layout | Sheets | Machine time | Glue time | Idle time | Total |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Template, Letter, page order | | | | | |
| Recreation, A4, colour order | | | | | |
| Recreation, A4, build-aware order | | | | | |

# Conclusion

A ready-made papercraft template is a good design delivered in a format that fixes paper size,
colour, piece count, tab width and build order. Recreating it digitally, with symmetry to make
the reading reliable and the folded mesh as the shared reference, lets the builder change all of
these for their own use while keeping the designer's shape.
